screens.body:
Security isn't a feature you bolt on at the end — it's a property of how you build. Every line of code that touches user input, money, or personal data is a security decision, whether you meant it or not.

Good news: you don't need to be a hacker to write secure code. You need habits. This course builds them.

options: Habits you build into how you code
check.question: Writing secure code mostly requires…

screens.heading: Security is a habit, not a product

screens.body:
The CIA triad is the foundation of all security thinking. C is Confidentiality: only the right people can see the data. Think medical records, passwords, private messages.

Break confidentiality and private things become public. Every login screen, every permission check, every encrypted message exists to protect confidentiality.

options: Only the right people can see the data
Hiding your code from your team
check.question: Confidentiality means…

screens.heading: C: Confidentiality

screens.body:
I is Integrity: the data hasn't been tampered with. When you transfer $50, integrity means it arrives as $50 — not $5,000, not $0.

Checksums, digital signatures, and database constraints all protect integrity. If an attacker can't read your data but can silently change it, you're still in trouble.
screens.heading: I: Integrity
screens.keyPoint: What you sent is what arrived.

screens.body:
A is Availability: the system works when legitimate users need it. A site knocked offline by a flood of junk traffic (a DDoS attack) has lost availability — even though no data was stolen.

Backups, rate limiting, and scaling all serve availability. The most secure system in the world is useless if nobody can reach it.

options: Working when legitimate users need it
check.question: Availability means…

screens.heading: A: Availability
screens.keyPoint: Secure AND reachable, or it doesn't count.

screens.body:
Threat modeling is asking four questions about your app before attackers do: What are we protecting? Who might attack it? How would they try? What stops them?

You don't need fancy frameworks to start. For SwiftGigs: asset = user payments; attacker = scammer; how = fake task to steal escrow; stop = verify identities, hold funds, review disputes.

options: What we protect, who attacks, how, and what stops them
check.question: Threat modeling asks…

screens.heading: Think like an attacker
screens.keyPoint: Ask the four questions before attackers do.

screens.body:
Your attack surface is every place untrusted input can enter: forms, URLs, APIs, file uploads, even HTTP headers. Each one is a door — your job is to make sure every door has a lock.

Smaller surface, safer app. That's why unused features, debug endpoints, and admin panels left public are classic breach stories.

options: Every entry point for untrusted input
check.question: Attack surface means…

screens.heading: Every input is a door
screens.keyPoint: Shrink the surface; lock every door.

screens.body:
Defense in depth means layers: if one defense fails, the next catches it. Validate input AND use parameterized queries AND limit database permissions AND log suspicious activity.

No single lock is perfect. A bank has a vault, cameras, alarms, and guards — your app deserves the same layered thinking.
screens.heading: Layers, not one magic lock
screens.keyPoint: If one layer fails, the next catches it.
